title: The p-Block Elements
description: Class 12 Chemistry The p-Block Elements (Groups 15-18): nitrogen family trends, ammonia and Haber process, oxides of nitrogen, nitric acid by Ostwald process, allotropes of phosphorus, phosphine and phosphorus halides; oxygen family, ozone, sulphuric acid by Contact process; halogens, interhalogens and oxoacids; and noble gases with xenon fluorides and VSEPR shapes, fully solved.

topics.title: Group 15 Elements
topics.concept:
Group 15 (the nitrogen family) contains nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), arsenic (As), antimony (Sb) and bismuth (Bi). The general valence-shell configuration is ns2np3 — a half-filled p sub-shell that gives extra stability and explains the resistance to losing or gaining electrons.

General trends

Down the group the atomic and ionic radii increase while ionisation enthalpy decreases; the +3 ion becomes more stable than +5 because of the inert-pair effect (the ns2 electrons become reluctant to bond). Common oxidation states are −3, +3 and +5. Nitrogen, being small and highly electronegative, shows the widest range (−3 to +5) and uniquely forms strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds, so it exists as the diatomic molecule N≡N. The heavier members cannot form pπ–pπ bonds effectively and so exist as larger single-bonded molecules (P4, As4).

Metallic character increases down the group: N and P are non-metals, As and Sb are metalloids, and Bi is a metal. The stability of the +5 state decreases down the group while the +3 state becomes more stable, so Bi(V) is a strong oxidiser.

Dinitrogen (N2)

Prepared in the lab by gently heating ammonium nitrite: NH4NO2 → N2 + 2H2O. The N≡N triple bond has a very high bond enthalpy (~941 kJ mol-1), making N2 chemically inert at room temperature.

Ammonia and the Haber process

Ammonia is manufactured by the Haber process: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 (ΔH = −92 kJ). Optimum conditions are ~200 atm, ~700 K and a finely divided iron catalyst with Mo as promoter. NH3 is a pyramidal Lewis base (lone pair on N) that turns moist red litmus blue and forms complexes such as [Cu(NH3)4]2+.

Oxides of nitrogen and nitric acid

Nitrogen forms many oxides: N2O, NO (neutral), N2O3, NO2, N2O5 — oxidation states +1 to +5. Nitric acid is made by the Ostwald process: catalytic oxidation of NH3 over Pt/Rh gauze gives NO, which is oxidised to NO2 and dissolved in water (4NO2 + O2 + 2H2O → 4HNO3). Concentrated HNO3 is a powerful oxidiser; with most metals it does not liberate H2 but gives NO2 (concentrated) or NO (dilute).

Phosphorus and its compounds

Phosphorus has allotropes: reactive white (P4 tetrahedra, stored under water), polymeric red, and layered black. Phosphine (PH3) is a weak base prepared by heating white P with NaOH. Halides PCl3 (pyramidal, sp3) and PCl5 (trigonal bipyramidal, sp3d) are made from P and Cl2; PCl5 is ionic in the solid as [PCl4]+[PCl6]-. The oxoacids include H3PO2 (1 OH, monobasic), H3PO3 (2 OH, dibasic) and H3PO4 (3 OH, tribasic) — basicity equals the number of P–OH groups, since P–H bonds are not ionisable.

examples.problem: Why does nitrogen exist as a diatomic gas (N<sub>2</sub>) whereas phosphorus exists as a tetra-atomic solid (P<sub>4</sub>)?
examples.solution:
1. Nitrogen is a small, second-period element and can form strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds because its 2p orbitals overlap effectively side-on.
  2. Two N atoms therefore form a stable N≡N triple bond, giving the diatomic molecule N2.
  3. Phosphorus is larger; its 3p orbitals are too diffuse for effective pπ–pπ overlap, so multiple bonding is weak.
  4. P instead forms three single bonds per atom, giving a tetrahedral P4 molecule which catenates into a solid.

Answer: Effective pπ–pπ bonding in small N gives N≡N (gas); poor pπ overlap in larger P favours single-bonded P4 (solid).

examples.problem: State the conditions used in the Haber process and explain, using Le Chatelier's principle, why a moderately high temperature (~700 K) is used rather than a very low one.
examples.solution:
1. Reaction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, ΔH = −92 kJ (exothermic, Δn < 0).
  2. Conditions: pressure ~200 atm, temperature ~700 K, finely divided iron catalyst with molybdenum promoter.
  3. Being exothermic, a low temperature favours a higher equilibrium yield of NH3.
  4. But at low temperature the rate is very slow, so the reaction takes too long to be economical.
  5. A compromise (~700 K) is chosen to obtain an acceptable yield at an acceptable rate.

Answer: ~200 atm, ~700 K, Fe/Mo catalyst; the moderate temperature balances yield (favoured by low T) against reaction rate (favoured by high T).

examples.problem: Arrange NH<sub>3</sub>, PH<sub>3</sub>, AsH<sub>3</sub>, SbH<sub>3</sub> and BiH<sub>3</sub> in order of (a) increasing thermal stability and (b) decreasing basic strength.
examples.solution:
1. Thermal stability of EH3 depends on the E–H bond strength, which falls as atomic size increases down the group.
  2. Therefore stability increases: BiH3 < SbH3 < AsH3 < PH3 < NH3.
  3. Basic strength depends on the availability/density of the lone pair, which is greatest on small, electronegative N.
  4. Hence basicity decreases: NH3 > PH3 > AsH3 > SbH3 > BiH3.

Answer: (a) BiH3 < SbH3 < AsH3 < PH3 < NH3; (b) NH3 > PH3 > AsH3 > SbH3 > BiH3.

examples.problem: Determine the basicity of H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> and explain the difference.
examples.solution:
1. Basicity = number of ionisable P–OH groups; P–H bonds do not ionise.
  2. H3PO2 (hypophosphorous): one P–OH and two P–H → monobasic.
  3. H3PO3 (phosphorous): two P–OH and one P–H → dibasic.
  4. H3PO4 (phosphoric): three P–OH and no P–H → tribasic.

Answer: H3PO2 is monobasic, H3PO3 dibasic and H3PO4 tribasic, set by the number of P–OH groups.

examples.problem: Why does PCl<sub>5</sub> behave as an ionic solid, and what is its structure in the vapour phase?
examples.solution:
1. In the solid state PCl5 exists as ions [PCl4]+ (tetrahedral) and [PCl6]- (octahedral).
  2. This ionic lattice is more stable than the molecular form in the condensed phase, so solid PCl5 conducts when fused.
  3. In the vapour (and liquid) phase PCl5 is a covalent molecule with sp3d hybridisation.
  4. Its shape is trigonal bipyramidal, with two longer axial P–Cl bonds and three shorter equatorial bonds.

Answer: Solid PCl5 is ionic, [PCl4]+[PCl6]-; in the vapour it is a covalent, sp3d, trigonal-bipyramidal molecule.

examples.problem: Concentrated nitric acid renders iron passive. Explain this observation and write the balanced reaction of dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> with copper.
examples.solution:
1. Concentrated HNO3 is a strong oxidiser and quickly oxidises the iron surface to a thin, adherent, unreactive oxide film.
  2. This passivating oxide layer stops further attack, so iron becomes passive in concentrated HNO3.
  3. Dilute HNO3 oxidises copper but liberates NO (not H2).
  4. Balanced: 3Cu + 8HNO3(dilute) → 3Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO + 4H2O.

Answer: A protective oxide film passivates iron; with dilute acid, 3Cu + 8HNO3 → 3Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO + 4H2O.

recap: Group 15 (N, P, As, Sb, Bi) has the configuration ns<sup>2</sup>np<sup>3</sup>; common oxidation states are -3, +3 and +5, and the +3 state becomes more stable down the group due to the inert-pair effect.
Nitrogen forms strong pπ-pπ bonds (N≡N gas) while heavier members do not, so phosphorus exists as P<sub>4</sub>; metallic character increases N (non-metal) → Bi (metal).

Ammonia is made by the Haber process (N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub>, ~200 atm, ~700 K, Fe/Mo); nitric acid by the Ostwald process (NH<sub>3</sub> → NO → NO<sub>2</sub> → HNO<sub>3</sub>).

Phosphorus allotropes: white (reactive P<sub>4</sub>), red (polymeric), black (layered); PCl<sub>3</sub> is pyramidal (sp<sup>3</sup>) and PCl<sub>5</sub> is trigonal bipyramidal (sp<sup>3</sup>d), ionic as [PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup>[PCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>-</sup> in the solid.

Oxoacid basicity equals the number of P–OH groups: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> monobasic, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> dibasic, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> tribasic; hydride basicity and stability fall down the group.

quiz.q: The catalyst (with its promoter) used in the Haber process for ammonia manufacture is:
quiz.explanation: The Haber process uses finely divided iron as catalyst with molybdenum (or K<sub>2</sub>O/Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) as promoter.

quiz.q: Which oxoacid of phosphorus is dibasic?
quiz.explanation: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> has two P–OH groups (and one P–H), so it is dibasic.

quiz.q: In the gas phase, the shape of the PCl<sub>5</sub> molecule is:
quiz.explanation: Gas-phase PCl<sub>5</sub> is sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridised and trigonal bipyramidal.

quiz.q: The correct order of basic strength of the hydrides is:
quiz.explanation: Lone-pair density is highest on small N, so basicity falls down the group: NH<sub>3</sub> > PH<sub>3</sub> > AsH<sub>3</sub> > SbH<sub>3</sub>.

topics.title: Group 16 & 17 Elements
topics.concept:
Group 16 (the oxygen family or chalcogens) is O, S, Se, Te, Po with configuration ns2np4. Group 17 (the halogens) is F, Cl, Br, I, At with configuration ns2np5 — one electron short of a noble-gas shell, so they are the most reactive non-metals.

Group 16 trends

Oxidation states range from −2 to +6; oxygen is usually −2 (no d orbitals, so no +6) while S, Se and Te show +2, +4 and +6. Atomic radius and metallic character increase down the group; O and S are non-metals, Se and Te metalloids, Po a metal. Hydride stability falls H2O > H2S > H2Se > H2Te while acidic strength rises in the same order. Oxygen forms strong pπ–pπ bonds (O=O), so O2 is diatomic, whereas sulphur catenates into S8 rings.

Dioxygen and ozone

Ozone (O3) is an allotrope of oxygen formed by passing a silent electric discharge through O2: 3O2 → 2O3 (endothermic). O3 is bent (bond angle ~117°) with resonance, and is a powerful oxidising agent (it liberates I2 from KI). It shields the Earth from UV radiation.

Sulphur and sulphuric acid

Sulphur exists chiefly as the yellow rhombic (α) and monoclinic (β) allotropes, both built from puckered S8 crown rings. Sulphur dioxide (SO2, bent, acidic, reducing) is made by burning S or roasting sulphide ores. Sulphuric acid is manufactured by the Contact process: S/ore → SO2; 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 over a V2O5 catalyst (~720 K, ~2 bar); SO3 is absorbed in conc. H2SO4 to give oleum (H2S2O7), then diluted. H2SO4 is a strong dibasic acid, dehydrating agent and (when hot/concentrated) an oxidiser.

Group 17 trends

Halogens have the most negative electron-gain enthalpies and high electronegativity (F is the most electronegative element). They are coloured, exist as diatomic X2 molecules, and bond enthalpy is Cl2 > Br2 > F2 > I2 (the small F–F bond is weak due to lone-pair repulsion). Oxidising power decreases F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2, so a higher halogen displaces a lower one from its salt.

Interhalogens and oxoacids

Interhalogen compounds XX′n (n = 1, 3, 5, 7) such as ClF3 (T-shaped), BrF5 (square pyramidal) and IF7 (pentagonal bipyramidal) form between two halogens; they are more reactive than the parent halogens. Chlorine forms the oxoacids HOCl, HOClO, HOClO2 and HOClO3 (hypochlorous, chlorous, chloric, perchloric) — acid strength rises with oxidation state. Hydrogen chloride (HCl) is made by heating NaCl with conc. H2SO4; its aqueous solution is a strong monobasic acid.

examples.problem: Explain why the bond dissociation enthalpy of F<sub>2</sub> is lower than that of Cl<sub>2</sub>, even though fluorine is the more reactive halogen.
examples.solution:
1. In F2 the two fluorine atoms are very small, so the F–F internuclear distance is short.
  2. This brings the three lone pairs on each fluorine into close proximity, causing strong lone-pair–lone-pair repulsion.
  3. The repulsion weakens the F–F bond, lowering its dissociation enthalpy below that of Cl2.
  4. The weak F–F bond is actually part of why F2 is so reactive — it breaks easily.

Answer: Inter-electronic (lone-pair) repulsion in the small F2 molecule weakens the F–F bond, so its bond enthalpy is lower than Cl2.

examples.problem: Describe the Contact process for manufacturing sulphuric acid with all balanced equations and conditions.
examples.solution:
1. Burn sulphur (or roast sulphide ore): S + O2 → SO2.
  2. Catalytically oxidise SO2: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, ΔH < 0, using V2O5 at ~720 K and ~2 bar.
  3. Absorb SO3 in concentrated H2SO4 to form oleum: SO3 + H2SO4 → H2S2O7.
  4. Dilute oleum with water: H2S2O7 + H2O → 2H2SO4. (SO3 is not absorbed in water directly because it forms a corrosive mist.)

Answer: S → SO2 → SO3 (V2O5, ~720 K) → oleum (H2S2O7) → H2SO4 on dilution.

examples.problem: Ozone acts as a powerful oxidising agent. Write the reaction with potassium iodide solution and explain the oxidation-state changes.
examples.solution:
1. Ozone oxidises iodide ion to iodine: 2KI + H2O + O3 → 2KOH + I2 + O2.
  2. Iodine changes from −1 (in I-) to 0 (in I2): it is oxidised.
  3. Ozone oxygen goes from 0 (effective) to −2 (in OH-): O3 is reduced, confirming it is the oxidiser.
  4. The liberated I2 turns starch blue — a standard test for ozone.

Answer: 2KI + H2O + O3 → 2KOH + I2 + O2; I- is oxidised to I2, so O3 is the oxidising agent.

examples.problem: Arrange HOCl, HClO<sub>2</sub>, HClO<sub>3</sub> and HClO<sub>4</sub> in order of increasing acid strength and justify the trend.
examples.solution:
1. The oxidation state of chlorine rises: +1 (HOCl), +3 (HClO2), +5 (HClO3), +7 (HClO4).
  2. More terminal O atoms withdraw electron density, stabilising the conjugate base (ClOx-) by delocalising its negative charge.
  3. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid.
  4. Hence acid strength increases with oxidation state.

Answer: HOCl < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4; greater O-count stabilises the conjugate base, raising acidity.

examples.problem: Predict the shapes of ClF<sub>3</sub> and BrF<sub>5</sub> using VSEPR theory.
examples.solution:
1. ClF3: Cl has 7 valence electrons; 3 are used in bonds, leaving 2 lone pairs → 5 electron pairs, sp3d.
  2. The two lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, giving a T-shaped molecule.
  3. BrF5: Br has 7 valence electrons; 5 bonds plus 1 lone pair → 6 electron pairs, sp3d2.
  4. One lone pair gives a square pyramidal shape.

Answer: ClF3 is T-shaped (sp3d); BrF5 is square pyramidal (sp3d2).

examples.problem: Why is concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> described as a dehydrating agent? Give one illustrative reaction.
examples.solution:
1. Concentrated H2SO4 has a very high affinity for water and can remove the elements of water from many compounds.
  2. It chars sugar by removing hydrogen and oxygen as water: C12H22O11 → 12C + 11H2O (absorbed by the acid).
  3. It also dehydrates formic acid: HCOOH → CO + H2O.
  4. Because it removes water rather than oxidising in these cases, it is acting as a dehydrating agent.

Answer: Its strong affinity for water lets it strip H and O as water, e.g. it chars sugar: C12H22O11 → 12C + 11H2O.

recap: Group 16 (O, S, Se, Te, Po) is ns<sup>2</sup>np<sup>4</sup>; oxygen is usually -2 while S/Se/Te show +2, +4 and +6; hydride stability falls and acidity rises H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>Te.
Ozone (O<sub>3</sub>) is a bent, resonance-stabilised allotrope and a powerful oxidiser (it liberates I<sub>2</sub> from KI); sulphur exists as S<sub>8</sub> rings (rhombic and monoclinic).

Sulphuric acid is made by the Contact process: SO<sub>2</sub> → SO<sub>3</sub> over V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> (~720 K), absorbed as oleum (H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>), then diluted; conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a strong dibasic acid, dehydrating agent and oxidiser.

Group 17 halogens are the most reactive non-metals; oxidising power F<sub>2</sub> > Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub>, but bond enthalpy is Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > F<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub> (small F<sub>2</sub> has high lone-pair repulsion).

Interhalogens (ClF<sub>3</sub> T-shaped, BrF<sub>5</sub> square pyramidal, IF<sub>7</sub> pentagonal bipyramidal) are more reactive than their parents; oxoacid acidity rises HOCl < HClO<sub>2</sub> < HClO<sub>3</sub> < HClO<sub>4</sub>.

quiz.q: The catalyst used in the Contact process for the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub> is:
The shape of the ClF<sub>3</sub> molecule according to VSEPR theory is:
quiz.explanation: ClF<sub>3</sub> has 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (sp<sup>3</sup>d); the lone pairs are equatorial, giving a T-shape.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the strongest oxoacid of chlorine?
quiz.explanation: Acid strength rises with the oxidation state of Cl; HClO<sub>4</sub> (Cl in +7) is the strongest.

quiz.q: Among the halogens, the one with the lowest bond dissociation enthalpy of the X–X bond is:
quiz.explanation: Bond enthalpy is Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > F<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub>; the large I–I bond is the weakest of all.

topics.title: Group 18 Elements
topics.concept:
Group 18 contains the noble gases: helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe) and radon (Rn). Except He (1s2), all have the stable closed-shell configuration ns2np6, which gives them their famous chemical inertness.

Occurrence and general trends

Noble gases are present in trace amounts in the atmosphere; argon is the most abundant (~0.9% of air). Helium is found in natural gas (from radioactive α-decay) and the universe at large. They are obtained by the fractional distillation of liquid air (He by separation from natural gas). All are monatomic, colourless, odourless gases with very low boiling points. Down the group, atomic radius and boiling point increase (stronger van der Waals forces) while ionisation enthalpy decreases — the falling ionisation enthalpy of the heavier members is what finally allows xenon to react.

Reactivity and xenon compounds

For a long time noble gases were thought to be completely inert. In 1962 Bartlett prepared the first compound, and only xenon (and to a lesser extent Kr and Rn) forms true compounds, because its large size gives a low enough ionisation enthalpy. Xenon reacts directly with the most electronegative element, fluorine, under different conditions:

  • XeF2: Xe + F2 → XeF2 (excess Xe, ~673 K, 1 bar).
  • XeF4: Xe + 2F2 → XeF4 (1:5 ratio, ~873 K, ~7 bar).
  • XeF6: Xe + 3F2 → XeF6 (excess F2, ~573 K, ~60–70 bar).

Xenon also forms oxides and oxofluorides by hydrolysis: XeF6 + 3H2O → XeO3 + 6HF, and partial hydrolysis gives XeOF4. XeO3 is an explosive solid and XeF6 is a strong fluorinating agent.

Structures (VSEPR)

The shapes follow VSEPR by counting lone pairs on Xe: XeF2 has 3 lone pairs and 2 bond pairs (sp3d) → linear; XeF4 has 2 lone pairs and 4 bond pairs (sp3d2) → square planar; XeF6 has 1 lone pair and 6 bond pairs (sp3d3) → distorted octahedral. XeO3 is pyramidal (one lone pair, sp3).

Uses

Helium fills weather balloons and provides an inert atmosphere for welding and a coolant for superconducting magnets (very low boiling point); a He–O2 mixture is used by deep-sea divers. Neon gives the red glow of discharge tubes and advertising signs. Argon provides an inert filling for electric bulbs and an inert atmosphere for arc welding of reactive metals. Krypton and xenon are used in high-efficiency and photographic flash lamps. Radon was once used in radiotherapy.

examples.problem: Why are the noble gases chemically inert, and why is xenon the most reactive among them?
examples.solution:
1. Noble gases (except He) have a completely filled ns2np6 octet, which is a very stable arrangement.
  2. Because the shell is full, they have very high ionisation enthalpies and almost zero electron-gain enthalpy, so they neither lose nor gain electrons easily.
  3. Down the group ionisation enthalpy decreases as atomic size increases.
  4. Xenon, being large, has a low enough ionisation enthalpy to be oxidised by the most electronegative element, fluorine, so it is the most reactive noble gas.

Answer: A stable filled octet and high ionisation enthalpy make noble gases inert; large Xe has a low ionisation enthalpy, so it alone reacts with F2.

examples.problem: Predict the shape and hybridisation of XeF<sub>4</sub> using VSEPR theory.
examples.solution:
1. Xe has 8 valence electrons; 4 are shared with F atoms in 4 bonds, leaving 4 electrons as 2 lone pairs.
  2. Total electron pairs = 4 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 6, giving sp3d2 hybridisation.
  3. The 6 pairs adopt an octahedral arrangement; the 2 lone pairs occupy opposite (trans) axial positions to minimise repulsion.
  4. The 4 F atoms then lie in one plane, giving a square planar shape.

Answer: XeF4 is sp3d2 hybridised and square planar (2 lone pairs trans, 4 Xe–F bonds coplanar).

examples.problem: Write the equations for the complete and partial hydrolysis of XeF<sub>6</sub>.
examples.solution:
1. Complete hydrolysis gives xenon trioxide: XeF6 + 3H2O → XeO3 + 6HF.
  2. XeO3 is a colourless, explosive solid.
  3. Partial (limited) hydrolysis replaces only some fluorine atoms: XeF6 + H2O → XeOF4 + 2HF.
  4. Further partial hydrolysis: XeF6 + 2H2O → XeO2F2 + 4HF.

Answer: Complete: XeF6 + 3H2O → XeO3 + 6HF; partial: XeF6 + H2O → XeOF4 + 2HF.

examples.problem: Why is XeF<sub>2</sub> linear whereas XeF<sub>4</sub> is square planar, despite both being xenon fluorides?
examples.solution:
1. XeF2: Xe forms 2 bonds and keeps 3 lone pairs, so there are 5 electron pairs (sp3d).
  2. The 3 lone pairs occupy the equatorial plane of a trigonal bipyramid, forcing the 2 F atoms axial → linear.
  3. XeF4: Xe forms 4 bonds and keeps 2 lone pairs, so there are 6 electron pairs (sp3d2).
  4. The 2 lone pairs go trans-axial in an octahedron, leaving the 4 F atoms coplanar → square planar.

Answer: The different number of lone pairs (3 in XeF2, 2 in XeF4) places them so that XeF2 is linear and XeF4 is square planar.

examples.problem: State two uses each of helium and argon, linking each use to the relevant property.
examples.solution:
1. Helium has very low density and is non-flammable, so it is used to fill weather balloons and airships safely (unlike hydrogen).
  2. Helium has an extremely low boiling point, so liquid He is used as a cryogenic coolant for superconducting magnets (e.g. in MRI).
  3. Argon is chemically inert, so it provides an inert filling for electric light bulbs, preventing oxidation of the filament.
  4. Argon also gives an inert atmosphere for the arc welding of reactive metals such as stainless steel and titanium.

Answer: He — balloons (low density, non-flammable) and cryogenic coolant (very low b.p.); Ar — bulb filling and welding atmosphere (chemical inertness).

examples.problem: Helium is found in natural gas though it is a noble gas. Explain its origin and why it is not obtained from liquid air like the other noble gases.
examples.solution:
1. Helium is continuously produced underground by the radioactive α-decay of heavy elements such as uranium and thorium, since an α-particle is a He nucleus.
  2. This helium becomes trapped in porous rocks along with natural gas, so natural gas can contain a few per cent helium.
  3. Liquid air contains only a tiny fraction of helium and helium has so low a boiling point that it would not condense at the temperatures used for fractional distillation of air.
  4. It is therefore far more economical to recover helium from helium-rich natural gas than from liquid air.

Answer: Helium comes from radioactive α-decay trapped in natural gas; its very low boiling point and low atmospheric abundance make natural gas the practical source rather than liquid air.

recap: Group 18 noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) have stable filled ns<sup>2</sup>np<sup>6</sup> shells (He is 1s<sup>2</sup>), giving high ionisation enthalpy and chemical inertness; they are monatomic gases obtained from liquid air (He from natural gas).

Only xenon forms a real chemistry because its large size lowers its ionisation enthalpy; it reacts with F<sub>2</sub> to give XeF<sub>2</sub>, XeF<sub>4</sub> and XeF<sub>6</sub> under different ratios and conditions.

VSEPR shapes: XeF<sub>2</sub> linear (sp<sup>3</sup>d, 3 lone pairs), XeF<sub>4</sub> square planar (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>, 2 lone pairs), XeF<sub>6</sub> distorted octahedral (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>3</sup>, 1 lone pair), XeO<sub>3</sub> pyramidal.
Hydrolysis: XeF<sub>6</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O → XeO<sub>3</sub> (explosive) + 6HF; partial hydrolysis gives oxofluorides such as XeOF<sub>4</sub>.
Uses: He for balloons, cryogenics and diving mixtures; Ne for discharge/advertising signs; Ar as an inert filling for bulbs and welding; Kr and Xe in high-power and flash lamps.

quiz.q: The first noble-gas compound to be prepared was made from:
quiz.explanation: Xenon, with its low ionisation enthalpy, formed the first true noble-gas compound (Bartlett, 1962).

quiz.q: According to VSEPR theory, the shape of XeF<sub>2</sub> is:
quiz.explanation: XeF<sub>2</sub> has 3 lone pairs (equatorial) and 2 bond pairs (axial), giving a linear shape.

quiz.q: The number of lone pairs on the central xenon atom in XeF<sub>4</sub> is:
quiz.explanation: XeF<sub>4</sub> has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>), hence square planar.
XeF<sub>6</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O → XeO<sub>3</sub> + 6HF; XeO<sub>3</sub> is an explosive solid.

questions.q: The valence-shell electronic configuration of Group 15 elements is:
questions.explanation: Group 15 has the half-filled configuration ns<sup>2</sup>np<sup>3</sup>.

questions.q: The catalyst used in the Haber process is:
questions.explanation: The Haber synthesis of NH<sub>3</sub> uses finely divided iron with a molybdenum promoter.

questions.q: Nitric acid is manufactured industrially by the:
questions.explanation: The Ostwald process oxidises NH<sub>3</sub> to NO to NO<sub>2</sub>, then to HNO<sub>3</sub>.

questions.q: The basicity of H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> is:
questions.explanation: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> has two ionisable P–OH groups, so it is dibasic.

questions.q: Which allotrope of phosphorus is the most reactive and is stored under water?
questions.explanation: White phosphorus (P<sub>4</sub>) is highly reactive and stored under water to prevent ignition.

questions.q: In the solid state, PCl<sub>5</sub> exists as:
questions.explanation: Solid PCl<sub>5</sub> is ionic, made of tetrahedral [PCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>+</sup> and octahedral [PCl<sub>6</sub>]<sup>-</sup>.

questions.q: The catalyst in the Contact process for converting SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub> is:
questions.explanation: V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> catalyses 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub>.

questions.q: Ozone is prepared by passing silent electric discharge through:
questions.explanation: 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2O<sub>3</sub> occurs in a silent electric discharge through dry O<sub>2</sub>.

questions.q: The correct order of acidic strength of the oxoacids of chlorine is:
questions.explanation: Acid strength rises with the oxidation state of Cl: HClO<sub>4</sub> > HClO<sub>3</sub> > HClO<sub>2</sub> > HOCl.

questions.q: Which halogen has the lowest bond dissociation enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Bond enthalpy order is Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > F<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub>; the large I<sub>2</sub> is weakest.

questions.q: The shape of the ClF<sub>3</sub> molecule is:
questions.explanation: ClF<sub>3</sub> has 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (sp<sup>3</sup>d), giving a T-shape.

questions.q: Hydrogen chloride is prepared in the laboratory by heating NaCl with concentrated:
questions.explanation: NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> + HCl on heating.

questions.q: Which of the following noble gases is most abundant in the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Argon makes up about 0.9% of air, the highest of the noble gases.

questions.q: The shape of XeF<sub>4</sub> according to VSEPR theory is:
questions.explanation: XeF<sub>4</sub> has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>), giving a square planar shape.

questions.q: The hybridisation of xenon in XeF<sub>2</sub> is:
questions.explanation: XeF<sub>2</sub> has 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs, so Xe is sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridised (linear).

questions.q: Complete hydrolysis of XeF<sub>6</sub> gives:
questions.explanation: XeF<sub>6</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O → XeO<sub>3</sub> + 6HF.

questions.q: Assertion: NH<sub>3</sub> is more basic than PH<sub>3</sub>. Reason: nitrogen is smaller and more electronegative, giving a more available lone pair. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true
questions.explanation: The smaller, more electronegative N concentrates lone-pair density, so NH<sub>3</sub> is the stronger base — R correctly explains A.

questions.q: Which noble gas is obtained mainly from natural gas rather than liquid air?
questions.explanation: Helium accumulates in natural gas from radioactive α-decay and is recovered from it.

questions.q: Concentrated nitric acid renders which metal passive?
questions.explanation: Concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> forms a protective oxide layer that passivates iron (also Cr and Al).

questions.q: Which species correctly matches its shape?
questions.explanation: BrF<sub>5</sub> has 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>), giving a square pyramidal shape.

questions.q: The total number of P–H bonds in H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> taken together is:
questions.explanation: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>2</sub> has 2 P–H, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub> has 1, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> has 0; total = 3.

questions.q: Which one of these is NOT a correct reason for choosing ~700 K (not a lower temperature) in the Haber process?
options: a higher temperature increases the reaction rate
the iron catalyst is most active around this range
a low temperature would shift equilibrium away from NH<sub>3</sub>
a low temperature would make the rate impractically slow
questions.explanation: The synthesis is exothermic, so a LOW temperature actually FAVOURS NH<sub>3</sub>; the moderate temperature is a kinetic compromise, making this statement the false reason.

questions.q: Among NH<sub>3</sub>, PH<sub>3</sub>, AsH<sub>3</sub> and SbH<sub>3</sub>, the hydride with the highest bond angle is:
questions.explanation: Bond angle decreases down the group with electronegativity; NH<sub>3</sub> has the largest (~107°).

questions.q: The number of lone pairs of electrons on the central atom in BrF<sub>5</sub> is:
questions.explanation: BrF<sub>5</sub> has 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>), giving a square pyramidal shape.

questions.q: Hot concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> reacts with copper to liberate:
questions.explanation: Cu + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(conc.) → CuSO<sub>4</sub> + SO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O; S is reduced from +6 to +4.

questions.q: Among the halogens, the one with the most negative (most exothermic) electron-gain enthalpy is:
questions.explanation: Chlorine, not fluorine, has the most negative electron-gain enthalpy; the small F atom has high electron–electron repulsion.

questions.q: The shape of XeO<sub>3</sub> is:
questions.explanation: XeO<sub>3</sub> has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (sp<sup>3</sup>), giving a pyramidal shape.

questions.q: Which reaction correctly represents partial hydrolysis of XeF<sub>6</sub>?
questions.explanation: Partial hydrolysis replaces some F by O: XeF<sub>6</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → XeOF<sub>4</sub> + 2HF.

questions.q: Assertion: the +5 oxidation state becomes less stable down Group 15. Reason: the inert-pair effect makes the ns<sup>2</sup> electrons increasingly reluctant to bond. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R true, R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.explanation: Down the group the inert-pair effect stabilises +3 over +5, exactly the reasoning given, so R correctly explains A.

questions.q: The interhalogen with a pentagonal bipyramidal shape is:
questions.explanation: IF<sub>7</sub> has 7 bond pairs (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>3</sup>) and adopts a pentagonal bipyramidal shape.

questions.q: Which property explains why F<sub>2</sub> is a stronger oxidising agent than Cl<sub>2</sub> despite a less negative electron-gain enthalpy?
options: low F–F bond enthalpy and high hydration enthalpy of F<sup>-</sup>
questions.explanation: The weak F–F bond and the very high hydration enthalpy of the small F<sup>-</sup> ion make F<sub>2</sub> the strongest oxidiser.

questions.q: On dissolving SO<sub>3</sub> in concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> during the Contact process, the product formed is:
questions.explanation: SO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (oleum), which is then diluted to give H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

questions.q: The brown gas evolved when copper reacts with concentrated nitric acid is:
questions.explanation: Concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> with Cu gives brown NO<sub>2</sub>: Cu + 4HNO<sub>3</sub>(conc.) → Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 2NO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O.

questions.q: The number of Xe–F bonds and lone pairs respectively in XeF<sub>4</sub> is:
questions.explanation: XeF<sub>4</sub> has 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs, hence square planar (sp<sup>3</sup>d<sup>2</sup>).
